title: Describe a time you built something from scratch vs using an existing solution: why did you choose that approach?
shortTitle: Describe a time you built something from scratch vs using an existing solution: why did you choose that approach?
keyPoints: Default to proven existing solutions; build custom only when the need is genuinely unique or core.
Weigh five factors: fit, time to value, total cost of ownership, control and differentiation, and risk.
The maintenance tail of custom code is the hidden cost juniors underestimate.
For security-critical functions like cryptography, always reuse vetted libraries.
Partial reuse is often best: buy the commodity parts and build only the thin unique layer.
Avoid not-invented-here syndrome: be proud of the code you did not have to write.
Show both directions if possible: reuse for commodity, build for differentiating capability.

s1_definition.oneliner: Default to proven existing solutions; build custom only when the need is unique or core to the business : and justify it with time, cost, fit, control, and maintenance.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Default to reuse** – Proven libraries and services are battle-tested and community-maintained.
- **Build for differentiation** – Build custom only when the capability is core intellectual property or a hard regulatory requirement.
- **Five factors** – Evaluate fit, time to value, total cost of ownership, control, and risk.
- **Maintenance tail** – Custom code is maintained by you forever; libraries are maintained by their community.
- **Security rule** – Never roll your own cryptography or security primitives.
- **Partial reuse** – Buy the commodity parts and build only the thin unique layer on top.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India needs a new safe. Buying a certified, battle-tested safe from a vendor is almost always smarter than welding one in-house. But if the bank invents a genuinely new kind of vault that is its competitive edge, building it in-house makes sense.

sections.s6_takeaway:
I have made the build-versus-buy call in both directions on the same project at National Bank of India, and that contrast shows how I decide. For retry logic on flaky downstream payment calls, I reused a battle-tested library because it is a completely solved commodity problem and the maintenance tail of custom retry code would have been mine forever.

For our fraud-scoring rules, I built from scratch because the rules encode the bank's proprietary risk model : no off-the-shelf product fit more than twenty percent, and this capability is core intellectual property. Building gave us the control and differentiation we needed.

The result was the best of both: we shipped quickly by reusing the proven library, and we invested custom effort only where it created real, unique value. We did not waste months rebuilding a commodity and we did not compromise our differentiating capability.

My default is to reuse for commodity and security-sensitive problems, and build only when the need is genuinely unique or core. I also weigh the long maintenance cost heavily, because that is the hidden price juniors underestimate.

Remember one sentence: Default to reusing proven solutions for commodity problems, and build custom only when the need is genuinely unique or core to the business.
